posts.cooked:
Hello Shopify Community!

I’m looking for technical guidance on a Shopify Flow workflow we’ve built for our small soap business. We’ve completed the workflow, but we’re holding off on activating it until we can confirm that inventory adjustments will execute reliably.

Our setup:

  • Shopify Basic plan
  • Appstle Subscriptions for recurring orders
  • Easify Product Options for customer soap selections
  • 13 individual soap products with Shopify inventory tracking enabled
  • Three subscription bundles containing 4, 8, or 12 customer-selected bars

How our workflow operates:

  1. Trigger: Order created
  2. Check whether the order has the FPC-Inventory-Processed tag.
  3. Identify orders containing a Front Porch Club subscription product.
  4. Loop through the order’s line items.
  5. Identify the subscription line item.
  6. Loop through its custom attributes (Bar #1, Bar #2, etc.).
  7. Match each selected soap name against 13 predefined conditions.
  8. Use Shopify’s built-in Send Admin API request action with inventoryAdjustQuantities to deduct one unit from the corresponding product’s inventory.

Each soap is mapped to its Shopify Inventory Item ID and our fulfillment Location ID.

We’ve tested the workflow using Shopify Flow’s simulation. The conditions correctly identify the selected soaps and reach the appropriate API action. However, the API mutations cannot be simulated, so we haven’t verified the actual inventory adjustments.

We have three technical questions:

1. Idempotency

Our workflow uses API version 2026-07.

The inventoryAdjustQuantities mutation requires an idempotency key using the @idempotent directive.

However, Flow’s built-in Send Admin API request action generates the GraphQL mutation automatically and only exposes an editor for the JSON mutation inputs.

Is there a supported way to provide the required idempotency key through this built-in action?

If not, does that mean inventoryAdjustQuantities cannot be reliably executed through Flow’s standard Admin API request action?

2. Accessing mutation errors

We understand that a GraphQL mutation can return userErrors even when the HTTP request itself succeeds.

We attempted to add a Condition immediately after the API request, but userErrors wasn’t available as a variable.

Can Shopify Flow access the userErrors returned by inventoryAdjustQuantities?

If so, what is the correct variable path or configuration?

3. Handling partial inventory adjustments

For a subscription containing multiple soaps, some adjustments could succeed before a subsequent request fails.

We want to avoid:

  • Deducting the same soap twice.
  • Marking an order processed when some adjustments failed.
  • Incorrect inventory counts when a workflow is retried.
  • Problems processing recurring Appstle subscription orders.

What is the recommended approach for safely handling these situations within Shopify Flow?

Our goal

Ideally, we’d like to keep this automation within Shopify Flow on our Basic plan rather than upgrade our plan or purchase another app.

We’re also open to a lightweight custom integration if the built-in Flow action cannot safely accomplish this.

Any guidance from developers familiar with Shopify Flow and the Admin GraphQL API would be greatly appreciated.

Thank you!

Hi, some things from my side:

From API 2026-04, inventoryAdjustQuantities need changeFromQuantity in every change. You can send null, but if you skip it the mutation fail. Your flow use 2026-07 so you need it.

For idempotency, i not see any field for key in Flow “Send Admin API request” in docs. Better test with hidden test product and one test order, then check run history. If it not work, small webhook app with key from order ID is more safe.

For partial problem, dont do one call per soap. Do one call per line item and put all soaps in changes array. Same soap 2 times = delta -2. And add your Processed tag after the API step, so if step fail the tag not added and the order not run twice.

userErrors is not Node, so Flow can’t give it to next step. If mutation fail the step fail and you see the message in run history.

Example inputs:

{
  "input": {
    "reason": "correction",
    "name": "available",
    "referenceDocumentUri": "{{ order.id }}",
    "changes": [
      {
        "delta": -1,
        "inventoryItemId": "gid://shopify/InventoryItem/YOUR_ID",
        "locationId": "gid://shopify/Location/YOUR_LOCATION_ID",
        "changeFromQuantity": null
      }
    ]
  }
}

Please test before live.

Hi there,

I’d be cautious about activating this workflow until you’ve tested the failure cases, because the main risk here isn’t the matching logic — it’s what happens if only part of the inventory update succeeds.

A few things I’d validate:

  • For inventoryAdjustQuantities, make sure every change includes the fields required by the API version you’re using. If changeFromQuantity is expected, don’t rely on simply omitting it without testing the actual Flow request.
  • I wouldn’t treat the FPC-Inventory-Processed tag alone as full idempotency protection. It helps prevent normal re-processing, but if the inventory request partially succeeds and the workflow fails before the tag is added, a retry could deduct the same component again.
  • If possible, send the component adjustments for a subscription item together in one mutation rather than making a separate request for every soap. That reduces the number of partial-failure points.
  • Only add the processed tag after the inventory mutation has completed successfully.
  • Test with a hidden product/order first, then intentionally create a failure condition so you can see exactly how Flow behaves on retry.

The userErrors part is also worth verifying carefully. Even if the HTTP/API request itself completes, GraphQL can still return mutation-level errors, so I wouldn’t assume “request completed” always means “inventory adjusted successfully.”

For this kind of workflow, I’d specifically test these three cases before going live:

  1. Full success
  2. One invalid inventory item/location
  3. Workflow retry after a partial or failed mutation

If those behave predictably, then the automation is much safer to trust for recurring subscription orders.

If you move this to a small webhook app, the order ID key stops the double deduct but not the miss. A failed delivery gets 8 retries over about 4 hours and then Shopify drops it, so one orders/create delivery is all you ever get. A sweep that runs every few hours and looks for orders with the Front Porch Club line item and no processed tag closes that gap, and the key is what makes the sweep safe to run that often.

Same reason the tag goes after the mutation rather than before. an order that failed stays untagged and the sweep picks it up. A tag written first makes the miss permanent.

Flow’s built-in “Send Admin API request” action hits a hard limit for this use case:

  1. Idempotency: Flow abstracts the GraphQL query envelope entirely, so you cannot pass the @idempotent directive or custom idempotency headers through the input editor.
  2. Response errors: Flow treated this action as fire-and-forget. It does not return the GraphQL response body (including userErrors) as variables to downstream steps.
  3. Partial failures: Because each loop iteration fires a separate request without rollback or response capture, Flow cannot guarantee atomic adjustments across multi-bar bundles.

To handle inventory deduction safely without duplicate deductions or partial syncs, you need an endpoint (such as a Cloudflare Worker or AWS Lambda) listening to the orders/create webhook. That lets you pass all bar adjustments in a single atomic inventoryAdjustQuantities call, handle userErrors, and tag the order once confirmed.

Good on you for not just flicking it on. One thing that might help while you test: make a saved view in Orders using the Not tagged with filter set to FPC-Inventory-Processed, plus the Product filter for your Front Porch Club item, and check it once a day. Anything sitting in there is an order the flow missed or choked on, so you catch it before your stock counts drift. Run it alongside your manual process for a week or two and compare. Out of curiosity, how are you doing the deductions by hand right now, straight in the product pages or from a spreadsheet?

ai_summary.summarized_text:
A soap business is delaying a Shopify Flow workflow that deducts customer-selected bars from inventory for Appstle subscription bundles, pending confidence that retries and failures will not cause stock errors. The workflow uses `inventoryAdjustQuantities` and a processed-order tag, but its simulation cannot verify actual mutations.

Replies say the mutation in API version 2026-07 may require `changeFromQuantity` on every change, and recommend validating the exact request with test orders. They also caution that Flow’s built-in Admin API action appears unable to accept an idempotency key or expose GraphQL `userErrors` to later steps; a successful HTTP request may not mean the inventory adjustment succeeded. Adding the processed tag only after the mutation and grouping bar changes into fewer requests can reduce risk, but the tag alone does not prevent duplicate deductions after partial failure.

Several replies recommend a small webhook integration to handle idempotency, mutation responses, and retries, with a periodic sweep for unprocessed orders to catch missed webhook deliveries. Before going live, test success, invalid inventory/location data, and retries after failure. A saved Orders view for eligible orders lacking the processed tag can support monitoring. No final implementation decision or verified test result is reported.
